newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian PM rejects Keating attack over race.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian PM rejects Keating attack over race.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday rejected criticism from his predecessor over his handling of a heated national debate on race and immigration and accused him of prolonging the row.

Former Labor prime minister Paul Keating, the architect of Asutralia's 1980s thrust into Asia, said on Monday evening that the race debate was "one of the saddest developments" in the country's recent history.
Keating also told a university audience in Sydney that it was the government's responsiblity to fight prejudice, not to watch opinion polls to see which way voters were leaning.
Asked on Tuesday about the speech, Howard said it simply prolonged the row -- which is already threatening to damage Australia's standing with its Asian neighbours.
"The debate I think is being kept going by frankly over-reactive speeches like last night," Howard said in a radio interview.
In his strongest public comment so far on the racism issue, Keating said the debate sparked by independent politican Pauline Hanson had let "a very ugly, resentful and xenophobic cat out ofthe bag".
Keating said Queensland MP Hanson, who has campaigned for an immediate halt to immigration and warned that Asians are swamping Australia, espoused "shamelessly regressive politics".
"The fact is that it is the responsibility of governments to protect the national interest against the tide of prejudice," he added.
Howard rejected the criticism: "If you really want something to sort of have less influence than you think it now has, I would have thought the most sensible thing to do is to ignore it."
"I don't believe this is a prejudiced country. I think we have some prejudiced people in it, we always have and we always will," he added.
A bipartisan parliamentary resolution two weeks ago reaffirming Australia's commitment to equal rights and non-discriminatory immigration has taken some of the emotion out of the race row.

But Hanson's comments and the debate they have stirred over the past two months have been blamed for a rise in official complaints of racism and a reported increase in abuse of Asian tourists and migrants.
Asians make up almost five percent of Australia's 18 million population and more than one third of the 100,000 immigrants each year.
Newspapers and commentators both at home and in Asia have criticised Howard for failing to quickly repudiate Hanson and bury the race row before it could take a grip.

Senior Australian ministers, including Howard's deputy, have warned the race issue could damage Australia's burgeoning A$73 billion a year (US$57 billion) trade with its Asian neighbours. Some tourist groups from Asia have already cancelled holidays to Australia.
Keating said Australia could "retreat to a past that never was, and create a future that can never be anything but third-rate".
"But if we do, we can be sure that the world will not be in a hurry to fogive us or bale us out," he added. "Even if they forgave us our prejudice, they could never forget our stupidity."
